text: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us and welcome to the Wayfair Q3
2026 earnings release and conference call. After today's prepared remarks,
we will host a question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question,
please press star one to raise your hand. To withdraw your question,
press star one again. I will now hand the conference over to Ryan Barney,
head of investor relations. Ryan, please go ahead.
Good morning and thank you for joining us. Today we will review our third quarter
2026 results. With me are Niraj Shah, co-founder, chief executive officer
and co-chairman, Steve Konine, co-founder and co-chairman, and Kate Gulliver,
chief financial officer and chief administrative officer. We will all be
available for Q&A following today's prepared remarks. I would like to
remind you that our call today will consist of forward-looking statements,
including but not limited to those regarding our future prospects, business
strategies, industry trends, and our financial performance, including
guidance for the fourth quarter of 2026. All forward-looking
statements made on today's call are based on information available to us
as of today's date. We cannot guarantee that any forward-looking
statements will be accurate, although we believe that we have been reasonable in our expectations
and assumptions. Our 10K for 2025, our 10Q for this quarter,
and our subsequent SEC filings identify certain factors that could cause the company's
actual results to differ materially from those projected in any forward-looking
statements made today. Except as required by law, we undertake no obligation
to publicly update or revise any of these statements, whether as a result of any new
information, future events, or otherwise. Also, please note that during this call we will
discuss certain non-GAAP financial measures as we review the company's performance,
including contribution profit, contribution margin, adjusted EBITDA,
adjusted EBITDA margin, and free cash flow. These non-GAAP financial
measures should not be considered replacements for and should be read together with
GAAP results. Please refer to the investor relations section of our
website to obtain a copy of our earnings release and investor presentation,
which contain descriptions of our non-GAAP financial measures and
reconciliations of non-GAAP measures to the nearest comparable GAAP measures.
This call is being recorded and a webcast will be available for replay on our
IR website. I would now like to turn the call over to Neeraj.
Thanks, Ryan, and good morning, everyone. We're pleased to be here to discuss our
third quarter results. Q3 was our strongest quarter of growth in the post-pandemic period,
with total net revenue up 9.7% year over year and our U.S.
business growing over 11%. That growth flowed through nicely to the bottom line
with an adjusted EBITDA margin of 6.9%, our best Q3 results since 2020.
At the start of this year, we told you we expected to take share in the U.S.
at a pace we had not seen in several years. We entered 2025 with the U.S.
share spread in the mid-single digits, widened it to high single digits by year end,
and promised to push it into the double digits in 2026.
With U.S. revenue growing double digits against a roughly flat category here in Q3,
we've done exactly that. That growth was driven by orders, which are up 12%
year over year. That translated to strength in customer growth with active customers
up more than 4% and new customer orders up over 14%, another
post-pandemic record. The momentum we have on orders and customers
gives us confidence that our share gains are structural because order growth
compounds over time while AOV growth does not. We're very excited by the
trajectory we're on and we're still in the early innings.
Earlier this year, I described the many pistons powering our engine of growth, and you're seeing their success
in real time as they work in tandem. We're frequently asked which of these
initiatives is the strongest link to our share success. The answer is that it isn't any single one.
Programs like Wayfair Rewards, Wayfair Verified, Delivery Plus,
our stores, along with long-standing businesses like Para Gold, our specialty retail
brands, and Wayfair Professional all sit on top of a core recipe of assortment,
availability, speed, and price that is the strongest it has been in our history.
Our core recipes are still early in their maturity and they compound on that core and on one another
to produce outcomes like we just delivered in the third quarter.
Let me give you an example of how that works in practice. A shopper walks into one of our stores
and discovers the depth of our catalog, including categories like bedding and tabletop she may never
have thought to buy from Wayfair. She joins Wayfair Rewards at checkout, giving her one more
chance to buy a product. Her kitchen table arrives in days rather than weeks because
we're sick close to our Castlegate fulfillment centers. And the next time she shops online, the verified
badge helps her choose with confidence. She comes back more often, she benefits from
low prices due to rewards, and for Wayfair, our ad costs have fallen, improving her customer
lifetime value. And as she helps our volume grow, suppliers invest more in our platform
and sharpen their pricing, which makes the offer even better for the next customer.
That's why we have real confidence that our U.S. share spread can keep building into 2027 and beyond.
You've heard us say this many times, but our success has been independent of the macro.
And when the category does return to growth, that spread will apply to a much larger base.
We're also following the same playbook now in our international markets, albeit at an earlier
stage with more to roll out in the coming quarters. Our approach remains the same.
Grow faster than the market, flow that growth through to maximize adjusted EBITDA dollars,
and keep reinvesting in what earns the customer's loyalty. The concept of
loyalty is a critical one to our flywheel. We began this year talking about loyalty in the scope of
our rewards program, and I now want to round out the year returning to the topic of loyalty and
how we think about it across our marketing investments. Over the past two years, we've
grown orders faster while spending less on advertising as a share of revenue, which was under
10% this quarter for the first time since 2021. This is even as we've invested
more in our brand and channels that are newer to the mix. So today I'd like to spend some time on what has
driven that progress, why we believe it lasts, and where we're headed.
The first driver is that more customers are coming to us directly. Rewards verified
our stores and a better, faster site and app all give customers
more reasons to start their shopping with Wayfair. In the third quarter, revenue from direct
visits was up more than 15% from a year earlier. That comes in tandem with
nice improvements in our core channels. For example, we've grown our text message audience by more than
40% over the past year, with revenue from those texts up by more than 30%.
The second driver is measurement, which has always been central to how we run
Wayfair. From our earliest days, we've built our own in-house tools to understand what every
marketing dollar returns, and that discipline is a big part of how we've stayed efficient.
Over the last few years, several things shifted at once. Privacy changes across
the major platforms made traditional attribution less reliable, and customer behavior
evolved in the post-pandemic environment, changing where and how people shop for their homes.
In response to this, we've significantly increased how often we test, leaning more heavily
on controlled experiments that isolate the true incremental impact of our spend.
Not surprisingly, that combination has surfaced opportunities to reallocate spend.
Where the spend was mostly reaching shoppers already on their way to Wayfair, we've pulled it back.
And where it reliably drives incremental sales, as with influencers, we're leaning in.
This is one of several factors that helped our conversion rate increase by more than 30 basis points
since early 2025. We've shifted more spend towards building the Wayfair brand,
with TV now a larger share of our marketing mix, including the fall campaign we launched in
September in tandem with the NFL season, and into newer channels like Creators and Video.
These investments build familiarity and trust in the Wayfair name,
and you can see it in how customers find us. Branded search visits, when a customer
types in something like Wayfair Sofa to a search engine, we're up more than 17% in Q3.
Every customer who comes to us directly is one we don't need to pay to reach again,
which frees up dollars to keep investing in growth. Creators are the clearest example of where we
ramped investment. Home is a category made for creator content. A product styled in a real home
answers the questions every shopper is asking, which is how it will look in her space.
So we built our program around what creators told us they needed, and we treat them the way we treat our suppliers.
We succeed when they succeed. And that work is paying off.
Sales driven by creator content grew more than 70% during this past
Wayday versus our event last fall. The program now includes tens of thousands of creators
who together with our partner networks have produced hundreds of thousands of new pieces of content this year,
far ahead of what we produced in 2025.
Creator program sales have already surpassed their full year 2025 total, and LTK, our largest
creator network partner, recognized Wayfair this year for leading what's next in creator commerce.
There's a lot we're excited for ahead, such as creator storefronts on the site and app,
which is set for a full rollout in 2027.
Creators are one example of how we are increasing our reach to make sure we are prominent everywhere a customer
may start their home shopping journey. These journeys can start in many places.
In a store, a social feed, a search interface, or an AI assistant.
Wherever her journey begins, we want Wayfair to be there and to make it easy for her to keep shopping with us.
In terms of AI applications and agents, our goal is simple,
and the same is how we think of other surfaces.
Wayfair's catalog should be available wherever shoppers are and optimized for the channel.
To that end, we're working across the major AI platforms and agent applications rather than betting on any single one.
We're confident that Wayfair is well positioned to compete here because we bring strengths we've spent two decades building.
The broadest selection in the category, rich and accurate product information,
customer reviews, competitive pricing, and fast, reliable delivery.
We share tens of millions of products with these platforms,
and we're using AI of our own to enrich that catalog data at scale.
While AI assistants are a new place for customers to start,
we're seeing that the destination is usually the same.
Most shoppers who discover us through these tools continue their journey on Wayfair's own site and app.
And even when a customer does buy inside an AI assistant, Wayfair remains the retailer.
We're a small company, and we own the delivery and service promise.
Either way, the relationship is with us. It's still early, but this traffic is growing quickly.
AI referred visits more than doubled sequentially in the third quarter to roughly 1% of our total traffic.
Much of our progress here comes from working hand-in-hand with the platforms themselves
and from partnerships with Google, OpenAI, and Meta, and these show what this looks like.
Google has been an important partner for nearly our entire history.
When Google set out to build an open standard for agentic commerce with the industry,
Wayfair was a foundational partner in co-developing the Universal Commerce Protocol.
Today, customers can find our products and even complete a purchase from Wayfair in Google's AI experiences.
We're also seeing many shoppers discover products in Google's AI experiences
and continue shopping on Wayfair's site, which helps us build lasting relationships with those customers.
With OpenAI, we were one of the first advertisers on ChatGPT
and one of the first to launch a Wayfair branded shopping agent that customers can chat with directly inside the platform.
Many conversations with our agent are multi-turn, and the most common request is help decorating or coordinating a room.
We're also seeing customers buy exactly the kind of inspiration-led shopping where Wayfair's assortment and design expertise stand apart.
When she's ready to buy, she completes her purchase on Wayfair.com, where her orders, her rewards, and her saved looks all live together.
So a conversation that starts in ChatGPT begins the beginning of a direct relationship with Wayfair.
We were also one of the first partners announced for Meta's Muse.
Our AI-optimized catalog is now live in Muse, and we're partnering with Meta to explore richer agent-led experiences.
So much home inspiration already starts in social feeds, and an assistant that helps a shopper turn that inspiration into a home she can actually buy is a natural fit for the breadth of our catalog.
The better AI agents get at helping customers navigate a vast, unbranded, and complex category like home, the more our scale, our data, and our logistics advantages come through.
Whether a customer first meets us through a creator, a search, or an AI assistant, our goal is the same.
To turn that first interaction into a lasting relationship so that the next time she's shopping for her home, she comes to Wayfair directly.

That loyalty is what has been driving our direct traffic higher as shoppers choose to come back to our site and app to have a shopping experience custom-tailored for the home category, and increasingly for that customer herself.

That is where much of our customer experience investment heading into 2027 is focused, making our site work more like a personal design partner with room ideas tailored to her style and complete looks built around what she's browsing, all anchored to inventory we can deliver.
That's the flywheel we're building. Every customer we earn, wherever she first finds us, becomes one who comes back to us directly, more often, and at a lower cost.
And that is what we believe will keep fueling both our share gains and our adjusted EBITDA growth into 2027 and beyond.
With that, let me turn it over to Kate to walk through our financials.
Thanks, Neeraj, and good morning, everyone. Let's dive into our financial results for the third quarter.
Revenue for Q3 grew by 9.7% year over year, with the U.S. segment up by 11.4% and our international segment down by 2.3%.

As we discussed last quarter, our international markets are in earlier stages of share capture than our U.S. business, and the home furnishings category in Canada and the U.K. continues to lag the U.S. market.
Orders were up by 12.2% versus the third quarter of last year, while AOV contracted by roughly 2%.
Most of the decline was driven by various facets of mix shift as the spread between the Wayfair.com business and our other higher AOV business lines narrowed.

Let me continue to walk down the P&L. As I do, please note that the remaining financials include depreciation and amortization, but exclude equity-based compensation, related taxes, and other adjustments.
I will use the same basis when discussing our outlook as well.
Gross margin for the third quarter was 29.6% of net revenue, driven by investments we continue to make into loyalty and the broader customer experience.
Customer service and merchant fees were 3.7% of net revenue, while advertising was 9.9% of net revenue.
As Neeraj called out, the first time we've had a single-digit result on this line since 2021.
The net of this was a contribution margin of 16.1%.
The progress we've made on advertising is a reflection of years of work as we've retooled our testing and expanded our channel portfolio.

We'll get to guidance in a moment, but some of the advertising cost outperformance here in Q3 was also a function of timing, and we would expect this number to come back up in Q4 as we lean in ahead of the holiday season.
Selling, operations, technology, general and administrative expenses were $378 million in the third quarter.
This came in slightly higher than our guided range as we saw a few one-time costs hit in the quarter, including the competition and markets authority settlement in the UK.
Reflecting the one-time nature, we fully expect to return to a range of $360 to $370 million next quarter.
That didn't stop us from delivering one of our most profitable quarters in history with adjusted EBITDA of $236 million for a 6.9% margin on net revenue.
Working to the bottom of the P&L, we delivered $62 million of net income here in Q3, a more than $160 million improvement compared to the third quarter of last year.
On our last call, we shared an in-depth breakdown of the bridge between producing positive adjusted EBITDA and positive net income, and we're pleased to see that play out here in Q3.
We ended the third quarter with $1.1 billion of cash and equivalents on our balance sheet and $1.5 billion of total liquidity when including a revolving credit facility.

Cash from operations was $198 million while capital expenditures were $62 million for free cash flow generation of $136 million in the quarter, more than 40% higher than what we produced in the third quarter of 2025.

While we had less activity on the capital markets front this quarter, I would be remiss if I didn't call out the double upgrades we received from both S&P and Moody's, matching what we received from Fitch earlier in the spring.
We talked at some length about our capital structure priorities on the last call, and part of that included a transition from repurchasing our convertible bonds to repurchasing our equity outright.
Q3 marked the beginning of that. We repurchased $60 million of shares at a full offset to the stock-based compensation we paid out in the quarter.
The result is a roughly flat share count quarter over quarter.
As we discussed, we intend to make this offset a recurring part of our capital allocation strategy while remaining opportunistic to modify when we believe it is appropriate.
Now let me turn to guidance for the fourth quarter. Starting with the top line, we would guide you to a high single-digit growth range for Q4.
We're pleased at the momentum we've seen to start the quarter, with Weyday last week nicely setting up the holiday events later this month.
Turning to gross margin, I would continue to guide you to the range of 29.5% to 30.5% of net revenue, once more targeting the lower portion of the range.
Customer service and merchant fees should be in line with what we delivered in Q3 as a percent of net revenue, and advertising should be in a 10.5% to 11.5% of net revenue range.
We do expect advertising as a percentage of revenue to come up in Q4 compared to Q3.

As I mentioned a moment earlier, there is some seasonality at play as we lean in heavier during the holiday season, but would still expect healthy year-over-year leverage on advertising versus what we reported in the fourth quarter of 2025.
SOTG&A should continue to be in a range of $360-370 million. Working your way down the P&L, we would expect adjusted EBITDA margin in a range of 6% to 7% of net revenue for the fourth quarter.

Now let me touch on a few housekeeping items. We expect equity-based compensation and related taxes of roughly $60-70 million. Depreciation and amortization should be approximately $59 million to $65 million.
Net interest expense of approximately $42 million. Weighted average shares outstanding of approximately $138 million.
CAPEX in a $70 million to $80 million range. You're beginning to see this line item grow as we ramp up our investment in stores, and that will continue into 2027.
Of course, this is all in the construct of strong performance from our stores, which allows us to self-fund that growth while still driving robust and growing free cash flow.
As we head into the holiday season and look ahead to 2027, I want to step back for a moment.
A year ago, we told you we would invest judiciously to grow the business at a rapid pace while growing adjusted EBITDA faster than revenue, and that is exactly what this quarter shows.

Our US share spread is now in the double digits. That growth is coming from orders and customers. We are spending less to acquire each of these customers, and more of each incremental dollar is reaching the bottom line.
In adjusted EBITDA, in net income, and in free cash flow. With a stronger balance sheet and a share account we are tightly controlling, we are turning that growth into more value per share.
Most of the initiatives Neeraj described are still early, and we believe the best of this compounding is still ahead of us.
Thank you, and with that, Neeraj, Steve, and I will take your questions.
We will now begin the question and answer session. Please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up.
If you would like to ask a question, please press star one to raise your hand. To withdraw your question, press star one again.
We ask that you pick up your handset when asking a question to allow for optimum sound quality. If you are muted locally, please remember to unmute your device.
Please stand by while we compile the Q&A roster. Your first question comes from the line of Simeon Gutman with Morgan Stanley. Your line is open. Please go ahead.
Good morning, everyone. Thanks for taking our question. So my first question is on loyalty.
Can you talk about how pleased you are with the level of growth you are getting and the level of, call it gross profit, dollar growth?
And Neeraj, is there a way to tell us the level of inning that you are with this? Does this completely change your ability to talk to consumers?
It feels like it is only a couple of quarters in. And I want to ask how much, I guess the share spread, are we early in the share spread equation?
Could that even grow even further? Thanks.
Thanks for your question. Yeah, let me start with loyalty. So on loyalty, I'd say we're very pleased. We launched it not quite, probably about two years ago.

And what we've seen is it's been growing at a nice rate. But to your question about innings and the growth ahead of us, the way to think about it is there's a lot that's ahead of us because you get sort of the folks who are paying the most attention, your most interested customers early.
But a lot of what we think is ahead of us is the program has very substantial benefits. And when we talk to customers about it, they get very excited about it.

It would still be relatively easy for a customer to be unaware of the program. And so if you think about all the places on our services where we can help existing members know of all the benefits, additional benefits they have so we get more dollars per year from them and gross profit dollars per year as you ask.
Or when you think about the much larger number of people who have not yet joined, where they can then learn about what the program is, the benefits they get, and then sign up.
And then once they sign up, the behavior changes because they want to take advantage of the program that they just joined. That's still ahead of us.
So I would say that we think we're, in terms of innings, it's not the first inning, but it's not far into the game, call it the third inning or something, second inning.
It's pretty early in the game. And we think this can ramp to be a much higher percentage of revenue than it is today.

And as you know, the core tenet of the program is that it offers the customers really tangible value in a way that encourages them to consider us much more top of mind as their go-to place for all things home, getting them buying across more categories.
The dollars per year go up. And our profit dollars per year go up because really the ad load associated with the revenue we get from that customer drops significantly.
So even though we're giving them benefits, we're net a winner on this.

In terms of how that ties in with share spread, how we think about share spread, we've talked now for a couple years about how when we entered 2025, we were at 0% year-over-year growth, which was taking share because the category was negative, but it was not a lot of growth.
And we talked about how we could go from zero to five, five to ten, ten to 15, 15 to 20, to 20 plus.

And we talked about how the recipe, price selection, speed availability was the foundation of how we've been taking shares since 2022, but that in 2025 we were now in a position where we could augment that with new programs because we've gotten far enough in the tech replatforming that we could allocate efforts then.
Rewards, loyalty, verified, delivery plus, some examples. Well, those have gone well. Those have helped accelerate our growth.
Now that we're even further into the replatforming and the big merchandising catalog change, we now, the whole concept of product-led growth can now get more cycles.

And obviously, agenda coding can even further accelerate that. And so the way we think about it is we're basically at ten. So we started talking about this at zero, zero to five, five to ten, ten to 15, 15 to 20, 20 plus.
We're basically at ten. And we're basically just marching along this agenda. So you're going to see that continue to happen.

And so from a share spread standpoint, we don't expect the categories growing at those rates, like stepping up at those rates. So the share spread is effectively the difference. You're going to see that continue to widen.
Okay. And then we're talking about EBITDA growth. And we talked about the outlook for this year being faster than revenue growth.

Is that a reframing going forward, a permanent reframing? We shouldn't think about margin anymore. We should think about dollar growth. And how does physical retail affect that growth rate one way or the other?
Yeah. So, well, I think ultimately the thing we're optimizing for certainly is EBITDA dollar growth. But if EBITDA dollar growth grows faster than revenue growth, the margin does expand over time.
But I think we want to focus on EBITDA dollar growth because EBITDA dollars can go up two ways. One is the margin rate expanding, but the other is the revenue dollars expanding.
And I think the way that you can actually get the furthest over any meaningful period of time is actually to think about both of those and not over optimize for the margin rate.

So the margin rate will continue to rise, but you're going to see the EBITDA dollars grow faster because on a relative basis between margin rate and revenue dollar growth, you're going to see the contribution from revenue dollar growth be quite high.

And, and so I mean, I'd add one, I think you mentioned that, you know, that is that a sort of a change or a shift that's actually, I think, pretty consistent with how we've talked about it for some time and how you've seen it play out, you know, for several quarters in a row now.

You also, I think, added how it's physical stores impacting this EBITDA dollar growth rate. And I think it's important to note that as we think about the stores, we're quite focused on the contribution of those stores.
And we're seeing, you know, as we talked about some really nice performance out of the Chicago market that's driving, you know, significant revenue growth there.

We're seeing really nice performance from the additional two stores. And so as we think about how that flows through the P&L, we're focused on that continuing to be, you know, over the long run still meeting that improved EBITDA dollar growth and improved EBITDA margin growth.
The stores themselves, we've long talked about those being self-funding. So as we think about the investment in stores on a capital perspective, that is well, we want to do in a self-funding way.
Okay. Have a great fourth quarter. Thanks.
Thank you.
Your next question comes from the line of Chris Horvors with JPMorgan. Your line is open. Please go ahead.
Thanks. Good morning, everybody.
I know you don't speak directly to quarter to date, but you did mention momentum.

We've seen some other categories that retail slow down based on, you know, the data points that we can see. We've had a very highly contested election, you know, the highest midterm spending of all time.
You've gas prices up. And so can you talk about what you've seen from the home furnishings market growth rate? Was there any sort of shake in the market here in October?

And any concern about the consumer? Or do you think there's some, you know, deferral of spending to post-election, especially as we think about the, you know, double digit share gains in three Q versus the high single digit guide for four Q?
Yeah, I think you're going to have two questions wrapped in there. Right. So one is like, how are we, how do we think the category is doing? And the second is how are we doing? Right.
And so I think if you break those apart, I think the category continues to bump along. And so, you know, it's a category that's been out of favor for some time. That's a very, very large category.
And it's cyclical, but we're probably on the low end of the cycle or at the bottom. And so, and we're seeing, we're not seeing any signs of it, you know.
It's basically bumping along. And that it's kind of been that way for a while. So I'd say consider that sort of, you know, holding the course it's been on.

In terms of how we're doing, we feel like we're doing quite well, but I think we're doing quite well for the reasons I mentioned earlier. Right. The recipe, what we're doing with product-led growth, what we're doing with programs.
And we feel pretty happy with our continued performance and our continued momentum. And it's not necessarily because the macro is changing at all. It's really because of the things we're doing.

Understood. And then on the advertising rate side, especially in light of the success that you're seeing in loyalty, if you went back to the IPO, I think you targeted a 6 to 8% margin rate on advertising.

You were a hair below that in the third quarter on an 80% repeat rate. As we think about potential advertising efficiency, to what extent does this rate come down over time back to that original goal as you build out the brand, as you mentioned.

And then to what extent is that improved tied to a higher repeat rate, which is wondering how that 80% compared to maybe some of the more established home furnishings brands out there in the retail world and how high that needs to go to maybe get that advertising rate down into that original 6 to 8.
Yeah. So for some of the modeling questions, let me, I'll turn it over to Kate in just one second, but just let me talk about the 80%.
So I think the way to think about the 80%, we're not particularly focused on the 80% meaning we want to grow repeat a lot and we want to acquire new customers. And the 80 is like the mix of the two.
And so if you're doing both equally well, the 80 would hold. Ultimately, if you get bigger and bigger, you might say there's less new customers to get. And so the repeat could grow.

I think at the end of the day, the repeat number should be pretty high because if repeat's not working, then the business is not working in retail. If you're not delivering your customers a good experience, they're not coming back.
Whether you have a problem in the near term or the midterm, you're going to have a problem. And so we tend to look at repeat on a narrower definition, which is our net repeat rate.
So different customer cohorts, how often are they coming back? And so it's not the metrics that are easy to see when you zoom out to the total because that has a lot mixed into it together.

But basically, we're seeing repeat strengthening and climbing, whether that's a more loyal customer or that's a relatively new customer to the brand, whether that's an e-com only customer, that's a customer, e-com customer who's then experienced stores and then what they do.
So we cut it up many, many ways. And so we're seeing that all going the right way, which is effectively the leading indicator of your future revenue and your future revenue growth rate.
In terms of how the guidance, the piano is shaped, let me turn it over to you.
Chris, I'm impressed that you can pull a model from 12 years ago that I'm embarrassed to say I was probably involved in developing. So thank you for the callback.
But as it speaks to sort of AC&R leverage, clearly we are seeing some nice momentum on AC&R leverage over the past 12 months.
And I think a number of the things that Neeraj mentioned are helping to drive that. So loyalty is something that should drive AC&R leverage and structural improvement over time.

Further order, volume growth and repeat growth, to your point, does drive AC&R leverage. And you see that start to show up and repeat order growth has actually grown quite nicely over the last several quarters.
Neeraj shared a stat on his call when he was talking about the marketing spend saying that revenue associated with direct traffic is up 15% year over year.
So you're seeing that momentum and that push that does help give more structural AC&R leverage.

That said, we do see some seasonality here. So I just want to remind folks that we sort of called out some of the improvements this quarter, maybe hit a little bit better because of the seasonality that we might see in the fourth quarter.
And, you know, we noted that obviously in the guide, but over time you have seen that nice engagement there.
Thanks so much.
Your next question comes from the line of Oliver Wintermantel with Evercore ISI. Your line is open. Please go ahead.
Thanks. Good morning, guys. So your contribution margin reached 16.1% despite lower gross margins.
And as we think about full Q&A next year, how much of that improvement is sustainable and where do you think you have to reinvest?
Yeah, Kate, why don't you?
I'll start. So the first thing I point to is, you know, we've talked for some quarters now about 15% being sort of a general place where we're operating contribution margin from.
Is that the right position to, as we talked about a few questions ago, really hit on that place of accelerating revenue growth and accelerating EBITDA dollar growth faster than that revenue growth?
So that 15% place seems to be generally, you know, sort of the right balance of trade-off on that gross margin and the AC&R.
Obviously this quarter you did see that accelerate a little bit.
Again, as we just talked about with Chris, some of that is due to the seasonality of the marketing spend.
And so in the guide, you know that that goes back to roughly that 15% place for next quarter.
I think the thing, just to zoom back out, right, we were talking a few minutes ago about EBITDA dollar growth and margin rate and what we're trying to do.
So think about the business. Ultimately, what we'd like to have is a very large business.
